paras: The killing of Orville Wright was the fatal shooting of a Black boy by William T. Cox, a Kansas City police patrolman, on a Wednesday afternoon in August 1910. Wright died in the city's old general hospital, and within days Cox was dismissed from the force and charged with first-degree murder.

According to a Kansas City dispatch dated August 22, Cox shot Wright, described as a "negro boy," on the preceding Wednesday afternoon, which fell on August 17. The boy's age is illegible in the surviving text of the report. Wright was taken to the old general hospital, where he died. The dispatch gives no account of why or where the patrolman fired, and it reports no statement from Cox.

Edward Curtin, the assistant county prosecutor, charged Cox with murder in the first degree in a complaint filed in the criminal court. A preliminary hearing was set for the following week in a justice court, and several witnesses were subpoenaed. Police Chief Griffin dismissed Cox from the force. No report of the hearing, an inquest or a trial was found.
In the same statement Curtin said he was preparing a charge of assault with intent to kill against Thomas Howard, a Black policeman who had shot a Black man on Vine street several weeks earlier.

The only report found ran on the front page of the Mena Weekly Star in Arkansas on August 25, 1910, under the headline "IS CHARGED WITH MURDER" and the deck "Policeman Who Shot Negro Boy to Have Hearing Next Week, Several Witnesses Subpoenaed." The brief item treated the case as court news, centering the prosecution and dismissal of the officer rather than the shooting itself. No coverage in Kansas City papers or in the Black press was found.
